848.title: Maddi in the forest
848.hook: Vessantara's wife comes home with fruit to find her children gone (Jataka 547)
848.howItsDone: Where the Vessantara tale is recited aloud, Maddi's chapter may be chanted slowly and with feeling, and audiences listen to it as part of a merit-making festival.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vessantara, read whole: the elephant, the exile, the gifts, the homecoming. Your line was the last life. Did you notice what one of your gifts cost? Today, the scene we left for later. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

A basket of fruit, roots and leaves, heavy on her hip. Maddi has been gathering in the forest all day, the way she does every day, so her children will have something to eat when she gets home. The night before, she slept badly, troubled by a frightening dream, and she told her husband about it. He told her not to worry. Now the light is going, and she is late. Something keeps standing in her path. Today, the Vessantara tale from the mother's side.
screen: `A BASKET OF FRUIT.` → `A BAD DREAM.` → `THE LIGHT IS GOING.`

segments.voice: First, the beasts on the path. In the tale, a lion, a tiger and a leopard stand across her road and won't move. The tale tells us what Maddi doesn't know: they're gods in animal shape, holding her back so she can't come home in the middle of the gift. She pleads with them to let her through, and only at nightfall do they step aside. Second, the empty hermitage. Every evening the children run out to meet her. Tonight nobody runs. She calls their names. She looks in the places where they played, by the pond, under the trees. Vessantara, sitting there, at first says nothing. Third, the long night. Maddi searches the whole night through, and at dawn she falls at her husband's feet as if dead. He sprinkles water on her face to bring her round, and only then does he tell her: he has given the children away to a brahmin, so that he might reach awakening. Fourth, her answer. The tale has her rejoice in the gift, and join her merit to his. Some readers find that ending hard to accept. Others hear in it a love that has already been tested by the worst night of her life. The tale does not hurry past her grief. It gives her search room to breathe, line after line, place after place. Tradition says that where the whole tale is recited aloud at festivals, Maddi's search is a part listeners wait for, and weep through. A story told for the sake of generosity stops, for a long time, to stand beside a mother looking for her children in the dark.
screen: `A LION, A TIGER, A LEOPARD.` · `NOBODY RUNS TO MEET HER.` · `SHE SEARCHES ALL NIGHT.` · `SHE REJOICES IN THE GIFT.` · then, large: `MADDI'S GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a parent's love. In Maddi's tale, love looks like worry: a late return, an empty hut, a search that lasts all night. Bring to mind a time someone who cared for you worried about you. A night they waited up, a call that came more than once, a face at the door when you finally got home. At the time it might have looked like fuss. Look at it now as care with nowhere else to go. If that relationship is a painful one, you can choose anyone whose care reached you. If it feels right, silently wish them well, wherever they are. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Maddi in the forest. The mother who came home with fruit and searched all night for her children. Today's word.
Your line: Maddi's grief. Today, when you hear someone's worry about a person they love, slow down and let them say all of it before you answer. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

what it means: the mother whose long night of searching gives the tale its grief.
what a scholar hears: the gods delay her on purpose so the gift can be made; the tale then slows down to follow her search, and that is the part of the recitation listeners are said to weep through.

849.title: Tales in stone
849.hook: Jataka carvings at Bharhut and Borobudur, paintings on the cave walls at Ajanta
849.howItsDone: Buddhist pilgrims walk around stupas and monuments with the shrine on their right, and at places like Borobudur the carved birth stories line the path they walk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maddi in the forest, searching all night for her children. Your line was Maddi's grief. Did you let someone say all of their worry? Today, the tales leave the page. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

A stone post, its faces carved with round panels. On one round panel, a deer kneels in front of a king. On another, monkeys cross a river on a bridge made of their own bodies. Next to some of the panels, a few letters are cut into the stone: the name of the tale. Somebody, long ago, wanted to make sure you knew which story you were looking at. This is the railing of a stupa at Bharhut, in India. Today, the Jataka told without words.
screen: `A CARVED STONE POST.` → `A DEER BEFORE A KING.` → `THE TALE'S NAME, CUT IN STONE.`

segments.voice: First, the labels at Bharhut. The carvers there didn't only show the tales; on some panels they carved the tale's name beside the picture. So a scene of animals and kings isn't a guess. The stone tells you which birth story it is, and scholars can match it with the tales we still read. Second, the walk at Borobudur. On the island of Java stands a huge Buddhist monument built in terraces, and its galleries are lined with carved panels, among them birth stories. Pilgrims walk around it, keeping the monument on their right, and the stories unfold beside them as they go, one scene after another, climbing level by level. You read it with your feet. Third, the painted dark at Ajanta. In western India, halls were cut straight into a cliff, and their walls were painted with scenes from the Buddha's lives. A white elephant among lotus pools, a prince and his court, crowds and palaces, all on rock. Fourth, why put tales in stone at all. A carving teaches anyone who can see, whether or not they can read. A monk or a parent could stand at a panel and tell the story while pointing to it. And stone lasts. The tales we have been hearing these weeks were told aloud, written down, copied, and also cut into rock and painted on walls in places far apart from one another. The six-tusked elephant you met a few days ago stands on a railing at Bharhut and on a painted wall at Ajanta. When you hear a Jataka, you are hearing something people once walked past, touched and pointed at.
screen: `THE NAME CARVED BESIDE THE PICTURE.` · `READ WITH YOUR FEET.` · `PAINTED ON THE CAVE WALLS.` · `A TALE FOR ANYONE WHO CAN SEE.` · then, large: `THE TALES IN STONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at one Jataka carving. If you have a screen nearby, find a photograph of one panel from Bharhut, Borobudur or Ajanta, and simply look at it for a little while. Who is in it? What moment did the carver choose? If you'd rather not look anything up, choose one tale from these weeks and picture it as a single carved scene: which moment would you cut into the stone? Then close your eyes and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Tales in stone. The birth stories carved and painted at Bharhut, Borobudur and Ajanta, for anyone who could see. Today's word.
Your line: the tales in stone. Today, notice one picture or carving you pass every day, and ask what story it was made to tell. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

850.title: The Jataka, closed
850.hook: the long road of many lives that the Jataka traces to one awakening
850.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use Jataka tales in sermons, schools and festivals, often telling a tale and then explaining which perfection it shows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tales in stone: Bharhut, Borobudur, Ajanta. Your line was the tales in stone. Did a picture you pass every day tell you a story? Today we close the book of birth stories. Day eight hundred fifty.

An elephant who carries a lost man out of the forest. A woodpecker who pulls a bone from a lion's throat. A treasurer who points at a dead mouse in the street. A caravan leader in the desert. A clever sage at court. A king who gives away his eyes. A prince who gives away everything. Different bodies, different times, different endings. In the Jataka, they are all the same one: the bodhisatta, the being on the way to becoming the Buddha. Today, the whole road at once.
screen: `AN ELEPHANT, A WOODPECKER, A TREASURER.` → `A SAGE, A KING, A PRINCE.` → `ALL THE SAME ONE.`

segments.voice: First, how each tale ends. In the Jataka, the Buddha tells a story of the past because of something happening in the present: a monk who's discouraged, a quarrel, a kindness. When the story is done, he names who everyone was. That monk was the frightened deer. That troublemaker was the jackal. And the wise one, he says, was I. That last line is what turns a fable into a birth story. Second, the road under the tales. Early in these weeks came Sumedha, lying in the mud before an earlier Buddha, setting out on the long way and taking on the perfections he would need. Every tale since then has been one step on that road: generosity here, patience there, truthfulness, effort, wisdom. Third, many shapes on one road. The bodhisatta isn't always a king or a sage. He's an elephant, a bird, a merchant, a minister. The tales let the one on the way to awakening be an animal or an ordinary worker. Fourth, where the road ends. The collection closes with Vessantara and the gift that cost him nearly everything. Tradition tells the life after it as the one in which he becomes the Buddha. So the Jataka doesn't end with an awakening. It ends right before one, with a family coming home from the mountain. Many lives, one direction. Some Buddhists read these stories as history, some as teaching tales, some as both. Read either way, the collection tells awakening as a long walk, made of small turns in ordinary lives.
screen: `AND THE WISE ONE WAS I.` · `ONE STEP AT A TIME.` · `AN ANIMAL, A MERCHANT.` · `IT ENDS RIGHT BEFORE AWAKENING.` · then, large: `MANY LIVES, ONE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick your favorite tale. Let the stories of these weeks pass by: the dead mouse, the monkey gardeners, the donkey in the lion's skin, the sky that was falling, the six-tusked elephant, Maddi in the forest. Which one stayed with you? Don't choose the one you think you should. Choose the one that comes back. Say its name to yourself, and in one sentence, why. Then let it rest and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The Jataka. The birth stories: one being across many lives, every tale a step on the road to awakening. Today's word.
Your line: many lives, one road. Today, tell someone the tale you picked, in two minutes, and see if it travels. Day eight hundred fifty.

851.title: The first council
851.hook: elders gather at Rajagaha after the Buddha's death: Ananda recites the discourses, Upali the discipline (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
851.howItsDone: Theravada monks still recite texts together in chanting sessions, and the tradition looks back to this first council as the moment its teachings were gathered and fixed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jataka, closed: one being, many lives. Your line was many lives, one road. Did your favorite tale travel when you told it? Today a new part begins: what happened after the Buddha was gone. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

The Buddha has died, and the monks on the road are weeping. One old monk named Subhadda tells them to stop. Don't grieve, he says. We're rid of that great ascetic who was always telling us what's proper and what isn't. Now we can do as we like. The elder Mahakassapa hears it, and he doesn't forget it. In the Vinaya, the book of monastic discipline, it is this remark that sets him to work. If the teaching isn't gathered now, he reasons, people like Subhadda will decide what it was. Today, the first council.
screen: `THE BUDDHA HAS DIED.` → `NOW WE CAN DO AS WE LIKE.` → `KASSAPA REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: First, the gathering. Mahakassapa proposes that the elders recite the teaching and the discipline together, before anything false can take root. The Vinaya says five hundred elders were chosen to meet at Rajagaha for the rains. Second, the one who almost wasn't there. Ananda had been at the Buddha's side for years and had heard him teach again and again, but he was not yet fully awakened. The text says he worked hard through the night before the council, and as he lay down to rest, before his head reached the pillow, his mind was freed. He walked into the council as one of the elders. Third, the questions. Mahakassapa doesn't ask for speeches. He asks questions, one at a time. To Upali, a former barber who had become an expert in the monastic rules: where was the first rule laid down? About whom? In what case? Upali answers, and the discipline is recited. Then to Ananda: where was this discourse given? To whom? And Ananda answers, and the discourses are recited. Fourth, what the word council really means here. The Pali name for it is sangiti, a chanting together. It wasn't a debate over new ideas. It was a room full of people saying the same words aloud, checking them against each other, so that what the Buddha taught would be held by many mouths and not just one memory. Some scholars ask how much of this account is history and how much is later telling. The tradition remembers it as the moment the teaching was gathered in, so it could be handed on.
screen: `RECITE IT BEFORE IT DRIFTS.` · `ANANDA, AWAKE JUST IN TIME.` · `UPALI ON RULES, ANANDA ON DISCOURSES.` · `A CHANTING TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE FIRST COUNCIL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite one thing you know. Choose something you carry by heart: a line from a teaching, a verse, a poem, a saying from someone who raised you. Say it once, quietly, at an ordinary pace. Then say it again, slower, hearing each word. Notice which words you're sure of and which ones wobble. That's how the elders checked their memory: by saying it aloud. Then let the words go and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The first council. Elders gathered after the Buddha's death to recite his teaching and his rules aloud, together. Today's word.
Your line: the first council. Today, when something important is said to you, repeat it back once to check you heard it right. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

fork.reveal: he remembers the remark and proposes that the elders chant the teaching and discipline together, before what is false can spread. the council grows out of one careless sentence.

original.note: Pali: a chanting together, a recital. the word used for the Buddhist councils.

trapdoor: what you thought: a meeting where leaders made decisions.
what it means: elders reciting the teaching together, question by question, so it would be held in common.
what a scholar hears: sangiti, a communal recitation; the account comes from the Vinaya's Cullavagga, and scholars weigh how much of it is history and how much is later telling.

852.title: Carried by memory
852.hook: for a long time, tradition says, the teaching was memorized and chanted by reciters, not written
852.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks and novices learn suttas and verses by heart and chant them together, and some monks learn whole collections.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first council: elders reciting the teaching together, question by question. Your line was the first council. Did you repeat something back to check you'd heard it right? Today, what happened to all those words next. Day eight hundred fifty-two.

"Thus have I heard." Open the Long Discourses at the beginning and that is how the first sutta starts, and the same words open sutta after sutta. Tradition says the voice is Ananda's, at the council, reciting what he heard the Buddha say. It's a strange way to start a holy text. Not: thus it is. Not: thus it was written. Thus I heard it. The teaching opens by telling you how it reached you: through someone's ears, and someone's memory. Today, how the teaching traveled before it was written down.
screen: `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` → `NOT: THUS IT WAS WRITTEN.` → `THROUGH SOMEONE'S EARS.`

segments.voice: First, the reciters. Tradition says that after the council, groups of monks took on different collections of the teaching and learned them by heart, chanting them together and teaching them to their students, who taught their own. A text was not a book on a shelf. It was a group of people who could say it. Second, a teaching built to be remembered. Read the suttas and you notice the repetition: the same passage again and again, lists of three things, four things, eight things, whole paragraphs repeated with one word changed. On paper, that can feel slow. Out loud, it helps a memory hold its shape. Repetition works like the binding of an unwritten book. Third, the monk who kept his own. The Vinaya tells of an elder named Purana who arrived after the council was over. The elders invited him to accept what they had recited. He said it was well recited, but he would remember the teaching the way he himself had heard it from the Buddha. The text records his answer and moves on. Even in the first generation, memory came in more than one voice. Fourth, the writing down. The chronicles of Sri Lanka say that at last, in a time of hardship, monks there wrote the texts down so they would not be lost. Until then, tradition says, they had been carried in people. Heard that way, the long stretch before writing looks less like a gap than a kind of care: the teaching was kept alive by being said aloud, by people who had given their lives to it.
screen: `A TEXT WAS A GROUP OF PEOPLE.` · `REPETITION HOLDS THE SHAPE.` · `PURANA KEPT HIS OWN.` · `WRITTEN DOWN AT LAST.` · then, large: `CARRIED BY MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: memorize one line. Take the line from today: thus have I heard. Or choose a short line of your own, from a teaching or a poem you love. Say it aloud three times. Close your eyes and say it again without looking. If a word slips, look, and try once more. Then let it sit in you, and rest with the breath. Tonight, see if it's still there. The bell holds the time.
Carried by memory. The teaching held by reciters, chanted together and passed on by mouth before it was written. Today's word.
Your line: carried by memory. Today, say your memorized line once at midday and once before sleep, and notice if it changes. Day eight hundred fifty-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old book someone wrote down.
what it means: a teaching held in people, chanted together and passed from teacher to student.

853.title: The minor rules
853.hook: the Buddha allowed minor rules to be dropped, but no one asked which; the elders kept them all
853.howItsDone: Theravada monks keep the full code of monastic rules, minor ones included, and recite it together at regular gatherings of the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thus have I heard: a teaching held in people before it was written. Your line was carried by memory. Is your memorized line still there? Today, one thing nobody remembered to ask. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

Which rules are minor? It sounds like a small question. In the account of the Buddha's last days, he tells Ananda that after he is gone, the community may, if it wishes, set aside the lesser and minor rules. It's a generous permission. A teacher loosening his grip, trusting his students. But it comes with a gap in it, and at the first council, the gap opens. Today, the minor rules.
screen: `WHICH RULES ARE MINOR?` → `YOU MAY SET THEM ASIDE.` → `A GAP IN THE PERMISSION.`

segments.voice: First, the report. At the council, Ananda tells the elders what the Buddha said: the minor rules may be dropped. The elders ask the obvious thing. Which ones? Did you ask him? And Ananda says no. He didn't ask. Second, the guesses. The Vinaya lets us hear the elders trying. Some say every rule except the gravest ones is minor. Others draw the line a little higher, then higher again. Each answer is reasonable. None of them settles it, because the one person who could settle it is gone. Third, Mahakassapa's answer. He turns the question around. Lay people know which things are proper for monks, he says. If we start dropping rules now, they'll say the teacher's rules lasted only as long as the teacher, like smoke. So let us not add rules the Buddha didn't make, and let us not take away rules he did make. The elders agree. They kept them all. Fourth, the cost to Ananda. After the council, the elders name several things Ananda did wrong, and failing to ask which rules were minor is one of them. Ananda says he didn't see it as a fault, but out of trust in the elders he acknowledges it. Some readers hear the elders being hard on him. Others hear the community choosing steadiness over its own best guess. Either way, the council kept the whole set of rules, and in the Theravada telling, that is why the small rules are still kept alongside the great ones.
screen: `DID YOU ASK HIM WHICH?` · `SOME DRAW THE LINE HERE, SOME THERE.` · `NOT ADD, NOT TAKE AWAY.` · `ANANDA ACKNOWLEDGES IT.` · then, large: `THEY KEPT THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one small rule. Choose one small rule you already live by, or used to: closing the cupboard, answering a message the same day, not eating at the screen. Something minor. Decide to keep it fully today, not because it's important, but because you said you would. Picture the moment it will come up. Then let the plan rest and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The minor rules. The Buddha allowed them to be set aside, but no one asked which, so the elders kept every one. Today's word.
Your line: they kept them all. Today, keep your one small rule all the way through, even when skipping it wouldn't matter. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

fork.reveal: Mahakassapa proposes keeping them all, so no one could say the rules lasted only as long as the teacher. the elders agree.

854.title: The second council
854.hook: a hundred years after the Buddha, at Vesali, a dispute over ten points, including handling money (Vinaya, Cullavagga 12)
854.howItsDone: Under the Theravada monastic code, monks are not to accept gold and silver, and lay stewards may look after money given for a monastery.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the minor rules. Your line was they kept them all. Did you keep your small rule all day? This week: Maddi's night, tales in stone, the Jataka closed, the first council, memory, and the rules nobody dropped. Today, a rule somebody bent. Day eight hundred fifty-four.

A bronze bowl full of water sits in the middle of the gathered monks. It's the observance day in the city of Vesali, and lay people are coming in. The monks ask them to drop coins into the bowl for the community. A visiting monk named Yasa watches this and can't stay quiet. Don't give, he tells the lay people. Gold and silver aren't allowed to monks. The Vinaya says this happened a hundred years after the Buddha's death. Today, the second council.

segments.voice: First, the trouble. The monks of Vesali don't take Yasa's protest well. They tell him he has insulted the lay people and must go and apologize. He goes, but instead of apologizing, he explains to the lay people why the Buddha forbade monks to take money. They're persuaded, and they side with him. Now the Vesali monks want him out. Second, the ten points. Yasa travels to find senior monks, and it turns out the coins are only one of ten practices the Vesali monks have allowed themselves. Most of them sound tiny: carrying salt in a horn so food can be salted later; eating when the sun's shadow has moved two fingers past noon; drinking palm juice that hasn't quite turned to wine; a sitting rug without a fringe. Small loosenings, each one with an argument behind it. Third, the elders decide. Senior monks gather at Vesali. To keep the meeting from turning into a shouting match, they hand the questions to a small panel drawn from both sides. The panel goes through the ten points one at a time, checking each against the rules, and finds every one of them not allowed. Fourth, what it shows. In this account, a hundred years in, the hard questions weren't about grand doctrine. They were about salt, sunlight and coins. The elders had promised to keep every rule. Here is what keeping that promise looked like: not a single dramatic heresy, but ten small bends, each one easy to explain, examined one by one. Tomorrow, what some say came out of this quarrel.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one small rule you bend. Not a big one. A small one you made for yourself, or agreed to: a bedtime, a budget, a promise about your phone. Find the place where you've let it slide a little, and the reason you give yourself. Don't scold. Just hear the reason clearly, the way the elders heard each point. Then let it go and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The second council. Elders meeting at Vesali, a hundred years after the Buddha, to judge ten small loosenings of the rules. Today's word.
Your line: the ten points. Today, when you hear yourself explaining why a small rule doesn't apply this time, pause and look at the explanation. Day eight hundred fifty-four.
